title: FlashProve: Zero-knowledge proofs of AI inference
story_key: story|title:flashprove zero knowledge proofs of ai inference
content_excerpt: Version 0.16.0 · A research artifact: not maintained, not accepting contributions. · Apache 2.0 FlashProve lets an AI provider prove which model answered a request, without revealing the model's weights. FlashProve runs Llama 4 Maverick at full size, with a 1,024-token context window, on a single NVIDIA H100. The prover reaches about 110 tokens/second of prefill at 24 requests per batch ( Performance ). The protocol's soundness is proved in Lean 4. A provider that tries to pass off output that is not the committed model's is caught, except with probability about q/2^124 + 2^-101 after q hash queries. lean/THEOREM.md has the theorem and how to check it. Building FlashProve, running it and checking its output take long builds and many exact comparisons. That work is meant for a coding agent. Point yours at this repository with: Run everything from the repository root as an ordinary user, never as root or under sudo . Only installing system packages needs root, so ask your user to do that. If root is the only account, create one first ( how ). Also read AGENTS.md for the rules on reporting results. It is silent for 1–2 minutes, then prints a line starting THE VERIFIER IS BUILT: and exits 0. A line starting build.sh: note: is a warning: quote it in your report. If your tool calls time out, run the build in the background: Then poll tail -n 2 verifier-build.log until the last line starts exit code . Don't start a second build meanwhile. Expect last line YES , exit code 0. This example is a small model with synthetic weights, so it shows only that the verifier works, not anything about a served model. Expect exit code 0, and the third line from the end starts AS EXPECTED: the honest copy was accepted . This builds cp_verify , cp_commit and cp_prove , then commits, proves one 64-token request and verifies it. Expect status 0 , a proof of work: line, then YES . Progress goes to $WORK/cp_commit.log . With too little memory it exits with code 2 at the start. For the real Maverick weights, see route 4 and examples/maverick/run.sh . To commit to and serve a model of your own, see Serving and the provider's duties . Those pages are required reading before using weights that must stay secret. verifier/docs/output.md has the full table. integrations/check_proof.py wraps the call and the comparisons. title: How We Optimized Browser Use for Deep Agents
summary: We compared seven browser toolsets for Deep Agents, picked Stagehand from Browserbase, and tuned it with LangSmith traces and evals. Here's what we learned.
story_key: story|title:how we optimized browser use for deep agents
content_excerpt: Browser agents can now take on multi-step work that's painful and time-consuming for people. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse plan cross-country road trips, cancel unused subscriptions, and list cars for sale, all on sites with no public APIs. DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Browser use helps in two places: actions an API can't cover, like using a website the agent wasn't set up for, and end-to-end testing of the web apps coding agents build. Either way, the agent needs two things: This post focuses on the tools, and on making them good enough that the agent uses the browser well. We set out to give agents in Managed Deep Agents a browser. We compared seven toolsets and picked the best one, Stagehand ( GitHub ) from Browserbase . Then we improved it based on what agents did in LangSmith traces, and validated every change with evals. The biggest lesson was how much room there is to improve an agent through tool design. Browser use toolsets come in a few forms: native tools, an MCP server , or a CLI the agent runs in a shell. Browser use poses two unique challenges for those tools: We iterated with the agent development lifecycle : run the agent on a benchmark, read its traces in LangSmith to see where it wasted steps or tokens, change the tool, and run evals to check that the change helped. Every run was a LangSmith experiment , so we could compare setups side by side and click from any number into the trace behind it. We had every harness return structured output (a JSON answer). That way a formatting slip, like a one-line reply to a task that asks for a table, didn't count against its browsing. We upstreamed that option to Browserbase's evals. We first held the model and tasks fixed and changed only the toolset. The seven toolsets differ in how the agent calls them: Every toolset passed between 78% and 90% of tasks, but cost and speed varied widely. The Stagehand tools passed the most (90%) for $1.98 in total, at a median 17.4 s per task. Playwright MCP passed 78% for $26.71, about 13x the cost, and took three times as long per task ( full results ). The gap held on harder tasks. On HardBench's 38 core tasks, Deep Agents passed 30 with Stagehand's code-writing run tool and 21 with Browserbase's command-style browse CLI, at three times the cost per task. Early browser tooling repurposed testing SDKs like Playwright . As Browserbase puts it, "Playwright was built for testing, we built Stagehand for your agent

title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put it his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. title: Why ctxd: Let the agent grep
story_key: story|title:why ctxd let the agent grep
content_excerpt: Frequent updates, tight budgets, latency targets. Fewer moving parts, fewer ways to break. Free software still uses compute and storage. The agent’s model can add usage charges with either approach. Speed depends on corpus size, hardware, caching and the agent’s search strategy. These are architectural trade-offs; end-to-end performance still needs benchmarking. You ask an agent how to roll back a deployment after its health checks fail. It finds a line about restoring the previous image. But the instruction immediately above it says to stop the rollout first. The agent needs a way to read beyond the match. Grep first search. No embeddings. That is our starting point for ctxd: searchable text, source paths and tools the agent can call again. ctxd’s local tracker keeps selected folders available through ctxfs. Your application gives the agent tools to inspect paths, search text and read source files. The agent chooses the queries. Embedding-based retrieval usually splits text into chunks, encodes them as vectors and maintains an index. Each layer brings decisions: where chunks end, which embedding model to use and how to keep the index current. We want to start with searchable text and source reads. Follow the same runbook through preparation, a question and a source edit. The weakness of grep-first search is the starting vocabulary. “Undo a deploy” may miss a file that says “rollback.” Searching for RUNBOOK will not find a file just because a reader would call it a runbook. Regex matches text patterns; it does not infer that meaning. Today, an agent can list folders and paths, read headings, and try alternatives such as rollback|revert|undo . It can use terms discovered in one source to search the next. ctxd exposes those operations; the calling agent supplies the vocabulary and judges the evidence. Our direction is to make that discovery loop easier to guide and inspect: choose a useful scope, try candidate terms, read evidence, then refine. Automatic vocabulary expansion is not part of the local search engine. The ctxfs guide describes the available read operations. A regex can find an error code, a service name or a phrase. The result gives the caller a file path and line number to inspect. In this example, searching for rollback finds line 3. Reading the surrounding passage reveals the step that comes before it. title: Show HN: MoEShift - Faster large MoE inference with half the RAM
story_key: story|variant:large,moe|title:moeshift faster large moe inference with half the ram
content_excerpt: Memory efficient and high performance Mixture-of-Experts inference for Apple Silicon 125 billion parameters. Up to 11 tokens per second. Under 10 GB of peak process memory. MoEShift is optimized for Apple Silicon: on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB of unified memory, it runs Qwen 3.8 Flash Next with roughly half the peak process memory of Strata and processes long prompts 2.6× faster. MoEShift leaves room for your other apps, helping your Mac stay responsive during inference instead of grinding to a halt under memory pressure. Keep browsing, writing and coding while the model works—all locally, with no cloud subscription. Alpha release. The core runtime is working, and the project is evolving quickly. You may encounter rough edges; your feedback helps shape the next release. Tested models and quantizations are listed below. Both use the shared SSD expert runtime on Apple Silicon. See supported architectures . Compared with Strata , a popular choice for local MoE inference, on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory . Both ran Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (125B), ISTA-DASLab GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS, with an 8,192-token context, no cached prompt tokens and 256 output tokens. Strata: 0.2.7, build 0.1.52. Time includes server-measured prompt processing and generation, excluding startup. Memory is macOS footprint -p peak physical process footprint. UD Q6_K XL on the same Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory. Medians of three measured runs after warmup, with no cached prompt tokens and 512 output tokens, using the benchmark runner . These runs use different output lengths from the Flash Next comparison above. The installation includes model preparation tools. MoEShift creates ~/.config/moeshift/config.json automatically on first launch and preserves your settings on subsequent launches and upgrades. Quantization is your choice: smaller files reduce storage and expert-cache memory; higher precision requires more space and memory. The benchmarks above apply only to the tested quantizations listed above. Download all shards of your chosen quantization into the same folder, keeping their names. Both models use the same preparation steps and the same ~/.config/moeshift/config.json ; each has its own entry under models . These two files total about 76 GB . Reuse them if already downloaded. MoEShift does not distribute or requantize models. Run this once to copy the model's specialized parts (“experts”) into files MoEShift can read directly from SSD. Keep all original GGUF files.

title: Claude Platform now supports native OpenTelemetry observability in Databricks MLflow
summary: An agent can return a plausible answer while missing an important finding or reading the same source repeatedly...
story_key: model:claude|title:claude platform now supports native opentelemetry observability in databricks ml
content_excerpt: Unify Claude observability into Databricks with native OpenTelemetry ingestion. Use collected traces with MLflow to find recurring failures and improve the agents. An agent can return a plausible answer while missing an important finding or reading the same source repeatedly. The answer alone won't explain why. Traces show the model and tool calls behind it, so you can investigate the failure, find related cases, and test whether a change helps. Databricks MLflow is now a supported destination for native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform.. With native export to Databricks MLflow, developers using the Anthropic SDKs, the Messages API and Managed Agents can send native traces to Databricks and use MLflow to debug their agents and evaluate changes. MLflow Tracing is built on OpenTelemetry, an open standard for collecting and exporting service signals. A trace records an agent’s execution as individual steps, called spans, such as model requests and tool calls. Claude’s native instrumentation generates these spans and exports them using the OpenTelemetry Protocol. Databricks receives the spans through Zerobus Ingest and stores them in Unity Catalog tables linked to an MLflow experiment. You can inspect Claude traces alongside traces from other instrumented services, with the same tools for debugging and evaluation. Unity Catalog controls access to the data, which you can also query with SQL. With the combination of Zerobus and Unity Catalog, enterprises can get two crucial benefits: low-latency trace ingestion at high QPS plus the ability to govern access to the sensitive data stored in agentic traces. In Databricks, open the Experiments tab and click Create Experiment . Under Trace storage location , keep Unity Catalog selected. Choose an existing catalog and schema. This creates new MLflow experiments linked to the Unity Catalog table that stores OpenTelemetry traces. The detailed setup guide covers permissions and SQL warehouse requirements. Set the Databricks destination using your workspace ID, region, and spans table. The Zerobus connection guide explains how to obtain a table-scoped OAuth token. The new native OTel integrations cover Anthropic SDKs, the Messages API, and Managed Agents. For the Anthropic SDK, install the packages below and configure an OTel tracer provider and exporter to create spans for Anthropic SDK calls. title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
story_key: story|title:statebench testing how language models track state changes over long documents
content_excerpt: We’re introducing StateBench , a benchmark for long-context state tracking —how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve. State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack. Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds. To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer. StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations: These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems –

title: Characterizing When Language Models Take Harmful Actions to Protect Their Assigned Goals
summary: Recent language model (LM) safety failures have largely been studied as disparate phenomena. In agentic misalignment, a model blackmails an executive to avoid being replaced. In alignment faking, it complies with harmful requests during training to keep its values from being modified. We argue that these behaviours share a common decision structure: a model assigned a goal must either take a harmful action to preserve it or refuse and lose it. We formalize this as a goal-harm conflict and present the same conflict under various elicitation protocols that range from compact forced-choice prompts to simulated agentic environments. These protocols span two perspectives on LM decision-making, which we term (i) the logit view, reading preferences from answer-token probabilities, and (ii) the sampling view, classifying open-ended responses with an LM judge. Under the logit view, we show that goal importance and harm severity additively shape how a model resolves these value conflicts. Under the sampling view, we derive two factorizations of the harmful-action probability that safety evaluations commonly report. The first measures how well a preference read from answer tokens carries over into behaviour, such as making a harmful tool call. The second attributes a low harmful-action rate either to refusal or to responses that reach no resolution. We then show how fictional context changes a model's preference under the logit view, and how tool use and partial observability -- two features of agentic evaluations -- change its harmful-action rate under the sampling view. Our work offers a descriptive framework for studying how LMs resolve such value conflicts and for estimating low-probability harmful actions at a finer granularity than the aggregate harm rates commonly reported in safety evaluations.

title: Networked Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web
summary: Several genuine AI services may repeat one unsupported source, and correcting that source may leave later reports unchanged. We examine these networked consequences of synthetic social engineering (SSE), deliberately misleading influence intended to redirect AI recipients from authorized objectives. Our framework connects social influence, information aggregation, and misinformation correction research to observable evidence and permission boundaries. It separates originating attempts from legitimate intermediaries' work and distinguishes identity, evidentiary support, and authorization. We test four relationships using Qwen3-4B and two briefing tasks across 1,080 research units in our Agent Service Exchange and Evidence Commons (ASE-EC). Multiple dependent publishers produced no supported increase in unsupported verification (78.3% versus 75.0%); publication availability left downstream violation reach at 40.0% in both arms. These comparisons direct attention to weaknesses already present in the reference workflows. High reference error rates and retained private handoffs preclude claims of immunity to social pressure. Without scope revalidation, corrections identifying dependent reports reduced residual invalid decisions from 14.4% to 8.1% at equal notification coverage and increased successful report repairs from 16/63 to 36/63. Scope revalidation added no demonstrated protection, and clearing dialogue offered no established recovery advantage. Unapproved requests persisted, all blocked by an external gateway. For designers, the findings caution against treating publisher count as independent evidence, notification as repair, or cleared histories as recovery. They support targeting corrections at reused reports, assessing factual and permission recovery separately, and enforcing authorization at execution.

title: MultiInpaintCOCO: Fine-Grained Visual Understanding in Multiple Languages
summary: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at https://github.com/ufal/multi-inpaint-coco.

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
